children: For a company committing capital to developing long-term port infrastructure, clarity on the operating horizon is a crucial requirement. At Gujarat’s Pipavav port, that issue appears to have taken centre stage. As a State government official puts it, “No company will consider making investments if they are not sure about their future.”

A recent “comfort letter” from the Gujarat Maritime Board (GMB) may have provided Gujarat Pipavav Port Ltd (GPPL) a measure of reassurance as it seeks an extension of its operating rights. The company now appears to be making the most of that signal, conserving cash as it prepares for what could be its next phase of expansion.

The letter is not an approval of the concession extension, but an indication of the way forward — GMB has asked GPPL to present, within 90 days, a detailed account of the port’s performance during the existing concession period, along with a fresh investment and business plan for the proposed extended tenure.

The company, which operates APM Terminals Pipavav, is preparing these submissions and expects to complete the process within the calendar year. Its immediate priority is to reach an agreement with GMB on the port’s investment plan and master plan. It then expects the board to communicate the next steps in the concession extension process.

“Considering the comfort letter received from the Gujarat Maritime Board, the board of directors have decided to start conserving cash for our future growth investments in the company,” Managing Director Girish Aggarwal told investors during a recent earnings call.
Plans in a limbo
The comfort letter, disclosed by the company in a stock exchange filing on August 26, marks a step forward, but the extension and its terms remain subject to discussions and regulatory decisions.

The development assumes significance given the scale of the company’s proposed expansion. In October 2025, GPPL signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding with GMB for investments of around ₹17,000 crore at Pipavav port. The plans include expansion of container, liquid and roll-on/roll-off (RoRo) cargo-handling capacities, as well as storage facilities and rail siding infrastructure.

GPPL operates Pipavav under a 30-year build-own-operate-transfer (BOOT) concession agreement signed with the Gujarat government and GMB on September 30, 1998. With the agreement set to expire on September 29, 2028, the company applied for an extension in 2011 and again in 2021, according to information provided by the Gujarat government in 2024.

Aggarwal did not offer any assurance on the eventual outcome or the timeline for signing an extended concession agreement. When an analyst asked whether the port’s operating rights could be put up for open bidding, he replied that the company was moving in the right direction but would remain cautious until the agreement was formally signed.

The decision to conserve cash has also translated into a moderation of shareholder payouts, with the board reducing the interim dividend to ₹3 per share. The company’s management team said the move was driven by the comfort letter and the anticipated expansion requirements, rather than the ongoing liquid jetty project, which is being funded through internal accruals.
GPPL pays GMB royalties linked to the volume of cargo handled at the port, which accounts for 3-4 per cent of its revenue, according to the management team.
Mundra awaits its turn

Beyond GPPL, the concession extension process has wider implications for Gujarat’s private port sector, especially since the operating agreements of many large privately developed ports approach expiry. After Pipavav, the next significant deadline is for Mundra — operated by Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone (APSEZ) — on February 16, 2031. APSEZ had submitted applications seeking extensions in 2015 and 2021.

The private port sector is closely tracking developments in the Pipavav case, as the outcome could determine the governing framework for future concession renewals. APSEZ Chief Executive Officer Ashwani Gupta, during the company’s second-quarter earnings call, indicated that discussions on Mundra’s concession were progressing, while making it clear that Pipavav was ahead in the process.

“It is going on very well. You already saw the comfort letter issued to Pipavav. I think it’s in the process. You will hear very soon from us. Because they are before us, so definitely they are ahead in the process,” Gupta told investors.

GMB has been discussing a policy framework for ports whose concession agreements are nearing expiry. The State government had also sought the Union government’s approval for the proposed framework, although there has been no formal announcement yet.

The issue is increasingly linked to the investment decisions of port operators. Infrastructure, such as deeper berths, mechanised cargo-handling systems, storage facilities and rail connectivity, requires substantial capital and long investment horizons. Uncertainty over the operating period can, therefore, lower the willingness of developers to commit fresh funds towards capacity expansion.
Peers with longer tenures

When Gujarat introduced its BOOT framework in 1997, it offered private developers an initial 30-year concession period before the assets reverted to the government, subject to the provisions of the respective agreements and extensions, if any. Since then, several other coastal States have moved towards longer concession structures to attract private investment in capital-intensive maritime infrastructure.

Ports such as Gangavaram and Krishnapatnam in Andhra Pradesh have concession structures offering potential operating periods of up to 50 years, while Kerala’s Vizhinjam port has a potential concession horizon of 60 years. Odisha has also adopted longer-duration arrangements for private port development. Gujarat, too, appears to be moving towards longer investment horizons for new maritime projects. Its recently announced shipbuilding policy allows waterfront concessions of up to 50 years for new shipyards. GMB has also indicated that the concession periods for six proposed greenfield ports in the State could range between 30 and 50 years, with the final tenure determined through the bidding process.

For now, the immediate test remains Pipavav. The company needs to complete its submissions, secure an agreement on the proposed investment and master plans, and seek greater clarity on the concession’s future before its ambitious expansion programme can move towards execution. The response to the proposal will be watched keenly by Mundra and other private port operators.

title: Pipavav port saves up to invest big
